etymology: From the Latin legatum, a bequest, through Old French legacie; that which is handed down from one generation to the next, especially the heritage of faith.
biblical_def: Legacy is that which a man hands down to those who come after him—most weightily, in Scripture, the heritage of faith, instruction, and godly example passed from one generation to the next. The Bible knows nothing of a legacy measured chiefly in goods; though a good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children, the inheritance that abides is the knowledge and fear of the LORD. The Psalmist sets the charge: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD… that the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children.” One generation is to praise God's works to another and declare His mighty acts. Paul saw such a legacy in Timothy, recalling the unfeigned faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice and was persuaded it dwelt in him also—three generations of faith handed down. The dictionary holds legacy to be a covenant duty: parents and the church are stewards of the deposit of truth, charged to pass it on entire, that the next generation may not have to recover what this one was given. It marks the word against two corruptions: the worldly legacy that measures a life by wealth, fame, or monuments—laid up for the just or scattered, but never the true treasure; and the sentimental legacy that wants to be remembered without handing down anything of substance. The legacy worth leaving is the faith once delivered, taught diligently to children, lived before them, and prayed into them—a torch passed from hand to hand until the Lord returns.
webster_summary: That which is handed down to those who come after, chiefly the heritage of faith and instruction passed from generation to generation (Psalm 78:4; 2 Timothy 1:5); a covenant duty, not the worldly measure of wealth or fame.

corruption_summary: The worldly legacy measures a life by wealth, fame, or monuments; the sentimental legacy wants to be remembered without handing down anything of substance—both miss the heritage of faith Scripture means.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the covenant duty of handing down the faith. The world measures legacy by what a man accumulates and the monuments that bear his name—wealth, reputation, achievement. Scripture redirects the whole idea: a good man leaves an inheritance, but the inheritance that endures is the knowledge and fear of the LORD passed to his children's children. The legacy worth leaving is not laid up in stone or stock but written on the hearts of the next generation.

A subtler corruption is the sentimental craving to “leave a legacy”—to be remembered, to matter—without actually handing down anything of substance. But legacy in the biblical sense is not about being remembered; it is about faithfully transmitting the deposit of truth. The Psalmist's generation showed the next the praises of the LORD; Lois and Eunice handed Timothy a faith that became his own. The dictionary recovers legacy as a stewardship: parents and the church are charged to pass on the faith entire, teaching it diligently and living it before the young, that the generation to come need not recover what this one was freely given.
roots_summary: From the Latin legatum (a bequest, from legare, to appoint or bequeath); the biblical idea is carried by nachalah (Hebrew, inheritance) and the handing-down of the covenant from generation to generation.
roots_lines: Legatum, Latin, a bequest, from legare, to appoint or bequeath.
Nachalah, Hebrew, an inheritance or heritage, often the covenant portion.
Dor le-dor, “generation to generation,” the biblical pattern of handing down.
Paratheke, Greek, the “deposit” of truth to be guarded and passed on (2 Timothy 1:14).
The godly heritage outweighs the material inheritance (Proverbs 13:22).
usage: The father labored to leave his children not chiefly an estate but the legacy of a living faith.
She saw in Lois and Eunice the legacy worth leaving: three generations of unfeigned faith.
The pastor charged the church to hand down the deposit entire, that the next generation need not recover it.

etymology: From “passionate” (Latin passio, suffering, strong feeling) and “prayer”; the fervent, wrestling, whole-hearted prayer that Scripture commends as effectual.
biblical_def: Passionate prayer is the fervent, earnest, whole-hearted pleading with God that Scripture commends as effectual—not the babbling of vain repetition, but the wrestling of a soul that will not let go. James gives the charter: “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much,” and points to Elijah, a man of like passions, who prayed earnestly and shut and opened the heavens. The supreme pattern is the Lord Himself in Gethsemane, who, being in an agony, prayed more earnestly, His sweat as it were great drops of blood. Jacob wrestled until the breaking of the day and said, “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.” Epaphras labored fervently in prayer for the Colossians, that they might stand perfect and complete. The dictionary holds passionate prayer to be the ordinary temperature of a living faith: prayer that engages the whole man—mind, will, and affections—wrestling with God over sin, souls, and the advance of His kingdom. It marks the doctrine against two errors. The cold formalism that reduces prayer to a recited duty, drained of all fervor, is a denial of the very life of prayer; the dead heart prays no passionate prayer. But the opposite error must also be named: the charismatic and revivalist excess that mistakes emotional intensity, noise, or working oneself into a frenzy for true fervor. Biblical passion in prayer is not manufactured emotion but the earnestness of faith laying hold of God's promises; it may be loud as Hannah's silent moving lips were thought drunken, or quiet as a groan that cannot be uttered. The measure is not the volume but the faith, the importunity, and the conformity to God's will of the one who, like the Lord, prays “not my will, but thine, be done.”
webster_summary: Fervent, earnest, whole-hearted prayer that Scripture commends as effectual (James 5:16); the wrestling of Jacob and the agony of Gethsemane—not cold formalism, nor manufactured emotional frenzy, but the earnestness of faith laying hold of God.

“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much” (James 5:16).
Patterned by Christ in Gethsemane, who in agony prayed more earnestly (Luke 22:44).
By Jacob, who wrestled and would not let go without a blessing (Genesis 32:26).
Not cold formalism, nor manufactured frenzy, but the earnestness of faith.

corruption_summary: Cold formalism drains prayer of all fervor, while charismatic-revivalist excess mistakes emotional intensity and worked-up frenzy for true fervor; both miss the earnestness of faith laying hold of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is fervency grounded in faith. One corruption is the cold formalism that reduces prayer to a recited duty, drained of all earnestness—the lips moving while the heart is far away. Scripture rebukes it: the prayer that avails is fervent and effectual, the wrestling of a soul that will not let go. A faith that never prays passionately should examine whether it is alive at all, for the living soul cries out to God.

The opposite error, especially live in charismatic and revivalist circles, mistakes emotional intensity for spiritual fervor—measuring prayer by volume, working oneself into a frenzy, equating noise and feeling with faith. The dictionary distinguishes biblical passion from manufactured emotion. True fervency is the earnestness of faith laying hold of God's promises and submitting to His will, as the Lord in Gethsemane prayed in agony yet “not my will, but thine, be done.” It may be loud or silent—Hannah's lips moved without a sound and she was thought drunken—but its measure is the importunity and faith of the one praying, not the decibels. Passionate prayer wrestles with God like Jacob, and like Jacob bows to receive the blessing He gives.
roots_summary: From the Latin passio (strong feeling, suffering) and the prayer-words of Scripture: the Greek energoumene (“effectual, working”) and ektenos (“earnestly, fervently”).
roots_lines: Passio, Latin, strong feeling or suffering, the root of “passionate.”
Energoumene, Greek, “effectual” or “working,” of the prayer that avails (James 5:16).
Ektenesteron, Greek, “more earnestly,” of the Lord's prayer in agony (Luke 22:44).
Agonizomai, Greek, to strive or wrestle, of laboring fervently in prayer.
Jacob's wrestling (Genesis 32) is the Old Testament emblem of importunate prayer.
usage: The pastor called the cold congregation to passionate prayer, the fervent pleading that avails much.
He warned the young zealots that biblical fervor is faith laying hold of God, not worked-up frenzy.
She wrestled in prayer like Jacob, refusing to let go until the Lord should bless.

etymology: The name given to the revival among the youth and counterculture of the late 1960s and 1970s, whose converts were nicknamed “Jesus People” or, derisively, “Jesus freaks.”
biblical_def: The Jesus Movement was a revival that spread among the youth and counterculture of the late 1960s and 1970s, chiefly in the United States, sweeping many out of the drug culture, the hippie movement, and Eastern mysticism into a professed faith in Jesus Christ. Its converts, nicknamed the “Jesus People,” were marked by zeal, communal living, street evangelism, baptisms in the ocean, and a new style of worship music that became the seedbed of the contemporary worship movement. The dictionary treats the Jesus Movement with discriminating honesty, applying its rule for movements outside the confessional Reformed tradition: honor the genuine work of God, name the weaknesses. Much in it was a true mercy of God. Real conversions occurred; many who had been bound in addiction and despair were savingly changed, owning Jesus as Lord; and a generation that had rejected the establishment church was confronted with the gospel. The Spirit poured out His grace, as He has done in revivals before—and there is no new thing under the sun, for God has often made His people willing in the day of His power. Yet the dictionary also names the real weaknesses that attended it. Much of the movement was doctrinally shallow, suspicious of theology and the institutional church, and easily swept into the charismatic and later word-of-faith excesses; its experiential and anti-creedal instincts left many converts without roots, and not a few of its streams drifted. The dictionary's verdict is the balanced one: the Jesus Movement was a genuine season of grace that gathered a real harvest, weakened by a shallow discipleship and a charismatic enthusiasm that sound doctrine and a confessional church would have guarded. Its abiding lesson is that revival is God's gift, to be received with thanksgiving and shepherded with the Word, lest the harvest be lost for want of rooting.
webster_summary: The revival among the youth and counterculture of the late 1960s-70s, whose “Jesus People” converts came out of the drug culture into professed faith; a genuine season of grace, weakened by shallow discipleship and charismatic excess.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary applies its rule for movements outside the confessional Reformed tradition: honor the genuine work of God, name the weaknesses. Much in the Jesus Movement was a true mercy. Real conversions occurred; many bound in addiction and despair were savingly changed and owned Jesus as Lord; a generation that had scorned the church was confronted with the gospel. God made His people willing in the day of His power, and the harvest among the young was real. The dictionary will not despise a season in which the Spirit visibly worked.

Yet honesty requires naming the weaknesses. Much of the movement was doctrinally shallow, suspicious of theology, creeds, and the institutional church, and quick to embrace the charismatic enthusiasm and, in some streams, the word-of-faith errors that the dictionary elsewhere rebuts. Its experiential and anti-creedal instincts left many converts without roots, and not a few of its currents drifted into error or burned out. The dictionary's verdict is balanced: a genuine season of grace that gathered a real harvest, weakened by shallow discipleship and a charismatic excess that sound doctrine and a confessional church would have guarded. The abiding lesson is that revival is God's gift, to be received with thanksgiving and shepherded with the Word—for a harvest unrooted is a harvest easily lost.
